title: Part-source remove/prefer writes are scoped by the caller's partId on a table with no shopId, and nothing checks the argument is a string
description: removePartSource and preferPartSource prove ownership with ownPart(partId), which runs db.part.findFirst({ where: { id: partId, shopId } }), a filter query. The write then uses the caller's original partId and sourceId in partSource.deleteMany / updateMany, not the id the ownership query returned. PartSource has no shopId column (schema.prisma:436), so the partId filter is the only thing keeping the write in one shop. Server-action arguments are not type-checked at runtime (no typeof/zod checks anywhere in src/actions), so the write's scope depends on the argument being a plain string, and the code never enforces that. Most other actions happen to be safe because their writes go through findUnique/update({ where: { id } }) or use the DB-returned id. This pair is the exception.
failure_scenario: A signed-in user of shop A calls the server action with id arguments that are not plain strings. The findFirst ownership check still matches a part in shop A, and the following deleteMany/updateMany on PartSource, with no shopId to scope it, can reach supplier rows that belong to other shops on the hosted multi-shop install (deleting them, or flipping their preferred flags).
suggested_fix: Reject non-string arguments at the top of every server action (a small assertId helper, or zod). In these three actions use the id ownPart returns (p.id) in every write, and scope sourceId through the relation: deleteMany({ where: { id: String(sourceId), part: { id: p.id, shopId } } }). Better still, add shopId to PartSource, as AGENTS.md requires for business tables.
evidence: parts.ts:112-116 ownPart uses findFirst and returns p, but lines 135 and 142-143 use the raw partId/sourceId args: `db.partSource.deleteMany({ where: { id: sourceId, partId } })`, `db.partSource.updateMany({ where: { partId }, data: { preferred: false } })`. schema.prisma:436-448: PartSource has id, partId, vendor... and no shopId. A grep for runtime type checks (`typeof ... === "string"`, `z.string()`) in src/actions returns nothing. Found by reading the code only, not tested against the server.
verifier_notes: confirmed: Accurate and exploitable. ownPart(partId) does db.part.findFirst({where:{id:partId, shopId}}) and returns only p.id, but removePartSource/preferPartSource then write with the caller's RAW partId/sourceId: deleteMany({where:{id:sourceId,partId}}) and updateMany({where:{partId},...}). PartSource has no shopId (schema.prisma:436), so partId is the only tenant scope. Next.js server actions do NOT runtime-type-check args (confirmed: no typeof/zod in src/actions; Next's own data-security.md warns args 'can be easily modified' and are reachable via direct POST). Passing a Prisma filter object as partId, e.g. {"contains":""}, turns id:partId in ownPart into a string-filter that matches any part in the attacker's own shop (so ownership passes), and the same object in the PartSource write matches rows across ALL shops. This is the exact exception the reviewer identified; most other actions use the DB-returned id or where:{id} update. Impact: cross-tenant write/delete of any shop's supplier rows; a double-filter payload [{"contains":""},{"contains":""}] on removePartSource would delete every PartSource row platform-wide (large-scale data loss, pushing toward critical). Rated high: affected table is secondary (where-to-buy links; no money/PII/tickets).

title: The part page's Receive and Set count work on a partner's consigned item, and Add part tells users to do exactly that, so the partner gets paid for the shop's own stock
description: The scanner refuses to receive into or use a partner's consigned stock (scan.ts:49, 'it isn't received or used here'), and the spreadsheet import never imports into it (it creates '<number> (own)'). moveStock (part page Receive and Set count) has no consignLinkId check. createPart's duplicate check is case-insensitive and includes consigned items, so entering the same number with an opening quantity gives the error 'X is already in inventory. Open it and use Receive stock to add N.' That sends the user to the consigned item's Receive form. The scan station's 'add as a new part' link on a consigned refusal leads to the same place. saveCounts (count mode scans consigned items through lookup) and Set count also rewrite a consigned item's qtyOnHand without telling the owner. At the register every unit sold from a consigned part becomes a consignSale and a consign.sale message. Neither side caps sold at placed for a positive sale (register.ts:280-283; partners.ts:956-975), so the owner is credited, and the holder is billed on the statement, for goods the holder actually owns.
failure_scenario: A sewing shop holds 2 units of partner A's item XA-100 on consignment. It buys 4 of its own and types XA-100 (qty 4) into Add part. It gets 'Open it and use Receive stock to add 4', opens XA-100 and receives 4, so qtyOnHand is 6. It sells all 6 at the register: 6 consign.sale units go to partner A and the monthly statement says the shop owes A for 6 units, 4 of which A never placed. Set count or Save counts on consigned stock also silently puts the shelf quantity out of line with the ConsignItem placed/sold/returned figures.
suggested_fix: In moveStock (and saveCounts) refuse, or route to the consignment screens, when p.consignLinkId is set, matching scanCode. In createPart, look for an existing own item with consignLinkId: null. When only a consigned item has the number, create '<number> (own)' as the import does, instead of pointing the user at the consigned item. Hide the Receive and Set count forms on consigned part pages. Optionally cap consignItem.sold at placed - returned for positive sales on both sides.
evidence:
Reproduced on localhost:3100 in my own shop (the part was marked consigned with SQL, as receiveConsigned would create it):
$ node t3.js
consigned part CSG-MUINLZ95 cmuinlzho00lzah7dif8ygfas
scanner receive -> ✗ CSG-MUINLZ95 is a partner's consigned stock: sell it at the register (it isn't received or used here).
add part same number -> ["CSG-MUINLZ95 is already in inventory. Open it and use Receive stock to add 4."]
db after part-page receive: 6|fake-link
moves: 4 RECEIVED
Code: parts.ts:82 `const p = await db.part.findFirst({ where: { id: partId, shopId: user.shopId } });` (no consignLinkId check) and parts.ts:51-53 (the duplicate lookup includes consigned items, then the 'use Receive stock' message).
verifier_notes: confirmed: This fix from round 1 is incomplete. Round 1 (8b3e5f2) made the scanner refuse consigned stock (scan.ts:49) and changed createPart to a case-insensitive duplicate check with the message 'use Receive stock'. It did not add a consignLinkId check to moveStock (parts.ts:80-108), and createPart's lookup (parts.ts:51) does not exclude consigned rows. Round 2 gave only the import the '(own)' handling (inventory-import.ts:70,105-107). So the app's own message sends the user to receive the shop's own units into the partner's consigned item. At the register, every unit of that item becomes a consignSale. consignItem.sold is incremented with no cap for positive quantities on either side (register.ts:280-283; partners.ts consign.sale only checks qty<0). The owner is therefore credited, and the holder billed, for units the owner never placed. The flow (consignment plus a number collision) is less common, but it produces wrong money between two shops.
also_reported_as: code: src/actions/parts.ts:80 Own stock can be received into a partner's consigned item; createPart tells the user to do exactly that

qa: src/actions/parts.ts:80 Own stock gets received into a partner's consigned item: the Add part message sends users there, and the part page Receive/Shelf count and the scan-station count skip every consignment guard

title: Spreadsheet import matches existing items only by exact part number, not by barcode or other numbers, so it creates duplicate items and splits stock
description: Before creating a row, importItems looks for an existing item only where partNumber equals the row number (or '<number> (own)'). It never checks the row's barcode against altNumbers or numberKeys, although the scanner, register and ticket lookups all match on numberKeys. A common path goes like this: a product is scanned, it isn't in parts, 'add as a new part' creates it with the UPC as its number, and later the supplier's line sheet (SKU + UPC) is imported. That creates a second item for the same product. The two items share a barcode, the delivery quantity and new prices land on the second one, and scanning the barcode keeps finding the first (exact-number match ranks first), which now shows the wrong stock and no price.
failure_scenario: Shop B: /parts?new=074427173148 > description 'Clover seam ripper', qty 4 > Add part. Then import [{SKU 3148, UPC 074427173148, 'Clover Seam Ripper', cost 4.10, retail 8.25, qty 6}]. Observed: 'added 1, updated 0'. Two items now exist: 074427173148 (qty 4, no price) and 3148 (qty 6, $8.25, alt 074427173148). Scanning 074427173148 reports '4 on hand' with no price. Expected: the row matches the existing item through its barcode and updates it (qty 10, price $8.25), or the import at least warns about the conflict.
suggested_fix: When no item has the part number, also look up own items (consignLinkId null) whose numberKeys contain numberKey(barcode) or numberKey(partNumber). If exactly one matches, update it and add the SKU as an alt number (or rename it). If several match, skip the row and list it in the result so the user can resolve it.
verifier_notes: confirmed: importItems (inventory-import.ts:67-74) matches existing items only by partNumber, or '<number> (own)'. It never checks the row's barcode against numberKeys or altNumbers. The path is ordinary: both the scan station (scan-station.tsx:194) and the register (register.tsx:196) link an unknown code to /parts?new=<code>, which makes the UPC the part number. A later line-sheet import (SKU + UPC) then creates a second item with the same barcode. Scanner and register lookups keep resolving the UPC to the first item (the exact-number match ranks first), which has the old stock and no price, while the delivery quantity and prices land on the duplicate.

title: The parts list stops at 1,000 rows before the low-stock filter and the value total, so low-stock items and the shelf value go missing for larger inventories
description: db.part.findMany({ take: 1000, orderBy: partNumber }) runs first. Only after that are 'Low stock only' (line 62) and the value total (line 63) computed in JS. A shop with more than 1,000 items (easy for a sewing shop: the import takes 5,000 rows at a time) gets a list that silently leaves out low-stock items after the 1,000th alphabetically, a header item count stuck at 1,000, and an understated '$ on the shelf at cost'. Nothing says the list is truncated.
failure_scenario: The shop has 1,003 items. The out-of-stock item 'ZZZ-LOW-1' (qty 0, reorder at 2) never appears under 'Low stock only', and the header reads '1000 items · $1000.00'.
suggested_fix: Do the low-stock filter in SQL, e.g. a raw `WHERE "qtyOnHand" <= "reorderAt"` or a Prisma field-reference comparison. Compute the count and the value with an aggregate query over all of the shop's parts. Page the list, or show 'showing 1,000 of N'.
evidence:
Reproduced in my own shop (1,004 parts, 1 of them low):
db: 1004|1
/parts header: 1000 items · $1000.00 on the shelf at cost
/parts?low=1 header: 0 items · $0.00 on the shelf at cost | shows ZZZ-LOW-1: false
verifier_notes: confirmed: parts/page.tsx:43-63 fetches take: 1000 ordered by partNumber, then applies the low-stock filter and the value total in JS. Anything after the 1,000th item is silently missing from the unfiltered list, from 'Low stock only' and from the shelf value. The repair dashboard (page.tsx:27) has no limit and does show all low-stock items, which covers repair shops. A retail-only shop is redirected from / to /register (page.tsx:32), so /parts?low=1 is its only low-stock view, and those shops are the ones with large imported catalogs (up to 5,000 rows per import).
also_reported_as: code: src/app/(app)/parts/page.tsx:62 Parts list truncates to 1000 items before the low-stock filter, total count and shelf value are computed
qa: src/app/(app)/parts/page.tsx:60 Parts list loads only the first 1000 items: item count, 'on the shelf at cost' value and 'Low stock only' are wrong for bigger inventories

title: One labels GET can render 9,000 barcodes (24 MB of HTML, about 14 s of server time)
description: The labels page takes up to 300 ids and up to 30 copies, and calls bwip-js toSVG once per label instead of once per part. Any signed-in user can make the server spend about 14 s and send 24 MB per request, and repeat it. (Checked: the SVG never contains the part-number text, includetext:false, so the dangerouslySetInnerHTML at :98 is not an XSS.)
failure_scenario: A signed-in user loops GET /labels?format=thermal&copies=30&id=<300 ids> and keeps a CPU core busy on a small hosted instance.
suggested_fix: Render each part's SVG once and reuse it for its copies, and cap the total labels per page (e.g. 600).
evidence: Measured in my own shop: `/labels?format=thermal&copies=30&id=<300 ids> -> 200 bytes 24284177 ms 13817`. Code: line 15 `.slice(0, 300)`, line 18 `Math.min(30, ...)`, line 21 `parts.flatMap((p) => Array.from({ length: copies }, () => p))`, line 95 `barcodeSvg(p.partNumber)` per label.
verifier_notes: confirmed: The reviewer describes the code correctly. labels/page.tsx:15 allows 300 ids, :18 allows up to 30 copies, :21 flattens to one label per copy, and Label() at :95 calls barcodeSvg (bwip-js toSVG, synchronous CPU) once per label, so up to 9,000 calls. Ids are limited to the user's own shop (:20), so an attacker only needs 300 parts of their own, which they can import. I reproduced it on my own instance of the same build. The impact is worse than 'keeps a core busy': the rendering is synchronous, so it blocks the Node event loop of the single next-server process. An unauthenticated GET /login sent 1.5 s later took 9.1 s. On the hosted multi-shop app, one signed-in user in any shop (and ALLOW_SIGNUP can make that anyone) freezes the whole service for every tenant for about 10 s per request, and can repeat it. bwip-js accounts for about 8.4 s of the 11.6 s, so the suggested fix (one SVG per part, plus a cap on total labels) removes most of the cost. The reviewer confirmed the dangerouslySetInnerHTML is not an XSS (includetext:false), and I agree. I raised the severity to medium under the rubric ('DoS needing auth') because it stalls all tenants, not just the attacker.

title: Labels page renders a barcode per copy with no overall cap (up to 300 ids x 30 copies = 9,000 bwip-js renders), and silently drops ticks past 300
description: Label calls barcodeSvg(p.partNumber) once per copy instead of once per part. Measured on the production build: 100 ids x 5 copies (500 labels) took 1.24 s and 1.1 MB. The allowed maximum is 18x that (about 20 s of server CPU and about 20 MB per request), which any signed-in user can repeat (DoS needing auth). The Parts list lets you tick up to 1000 rows, but the page keeps only the first 300 ids (line 15) without saying so.
failure_scenario: GET /labels?id=<100 ids>&format=thermal&copies=5 -> 1236 ms, 1.1 MB. With 300 ids and copies=30 the cost scales roughly 18x. Ticking 400 parts on /parts and pressing Print labels prints 300 with no notice.
suggested_fix: Compute the SVG once per part (a Map of id to svg) and reuse it for copies. Cap total labels (e.g. 600) with a visible 'first N shown' message, and show a note when more than 300 ids were sent.
evidence: e13.js: `100 ids x 1 copies: 200 350ms 0.3MB` / `100 ids x 5 copies: 200 1236ms 1.1MB`. labels/page.tsx:15 `.slice(0, 300)`, :18 `Math.min(30, ...)`, :88 `parts.flatMap((p) => Array.from({ length: copies }, () => p))`, :95 `const svg = barcodeSvg(p.partNumber);`.
verifier_notes: confirmed: The code is as described: ids are capped at 300 (labels/page.tsx:15), copies at 30 (:18), labels are expanded per copy (:21, not :88 as cited), and Label calls barcodeSvg for every copy (:95). bwip-js is synchronous, so this blocks the Node event loop for every shop on the install, not only the requester. It is a GET that any signed-in user (TECH included, and anyone at all when ALLOW_SIGNUP=true) can repeat or run in parallel. That is DoS needing auth, which the rubric puts at medium. Rendering one SVG per part would cut the maximum from 9000 renders to 300. The 'silently drops past 300' part is real but hard to reach: /parts has no select-all, so you'd have to tick 300+ boxes by hand.

title: Upload size pre-checks are bypassed by chunked requests; the server buffers the whole body in memory (300 MB grew RSS from 430 MB to 1.2 GB)
description: /api/library/file (150 MB limit) and /api/figures (2 MB limit) refuse large uploads only by reading the Content-Length header. They then call `req.formData()`, which reads the whole body into memory. A request sent with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` has no Content-Length, so `Number(null ?? 0)` is 0 and the check passes. Next's route handlers impose no body limit of their own (the 16 MB serverActions.bodySizeLimit applies only to server actions). The file.size checks run only after the body has been buffered. src/app/api/photos/route.ts:12 has the same pattern (outside my area). On the Windows program any signed-in device on the LAN can do this. On hosted, /api/figures and /api/photos are reachable by any user of any tenant, and memory runs out for the whole container.
failure_scenario: A signed-in user (any role) streams a few GB of chunked multipart to /api/library/file on the shop PC (or /api/figures on Railway). Node buffers it at about 2.5x the body size and the server runs out of memory. On the shop PC every device loses the app until main.mjs restarts it. On hosted, every company is down.
suggested_fix: Don't rely on Content-Length. Refuse requests that have no Content-Length (or Transfer-Encoding: chunked) on these routes, or stream-parse the body with a hard byte cap (e.g. busboy with limits.fileSize/fieldSize, or wrap req.body in a counting TransformStream that aborts past the limit) before calling formData(). Apply the same to /api/photos. On the Windows program, also cap the size and count of _inbox uploads per user.
evidence:
My instance on :6733, next-server pid 5927:
before: VmRSS 430136 kB
$ curl -b A.jar -X POST -H 'Content-Length: 300000000' ... /api/library/file  -> 'That PDF is too large. 413' (declared length is refused)
$ python3 chunked.py http://localhost:6733/api/library/file A.jar 300 file big.pdf  -> '413 That PDF is too large. (300 MB sent chunked in 1.8s)'
after: VmHWM/VmRSS 1202892 kB
$ python3 chunked.py http://localhost:6733/api/figures A.jar 30 box  -> '400 Bad box.' (30 MB parsed despite the 2 MB limit; with Content-Length it returns 413)
(script: scratchpad/agents/sec-files-lib/chunked.py)
verifier_notes: confirmed: The only size checks before req.formData() read the Content-Length header (figures/route.ts:10, library/file/route.ts:41, photos/route.ts:12). A chunked request has no Content-Length, so `Number(null ?? 0)` is 0 and the check passes. proxy.ts's matcher excludes /api, so proxyClientMaxBodySize buffering doesn't apply, and serverActions.bodySizeLimit covers server actions only. The file.size checks run after the whole body is in memory. All three routes require a signed-in user. On hosted, /api/library/file returns 404 before parsing because LIBRARY_DIR is unset, but /api/figures and /api/photos are open to any tenant's user, so one user can exhaust the memory of the process every tenant shares. This is DoS that needs sign-in, which the rubric puts at medium.
also_reported_as: code: src/app/api/library/file/route.ts:41 Upload size guards trust Content-Length: a chunked request is buffered in full by req.formData() (memory DoS for any signed-in user)
qa: src/app/api/library/file/route.ts:41 Upload size caps bypassed with a chunked request: any signed-in user can make the server buffer an unlimited body (round-1 fix incomplete)

title: FigureImage is a table shared by all shops: an owner or admin of any company can overwrite the factory-setting figures every other company sees (and any tech can plant the first copy)
description: FigureImage (prisma/schema.prisma:535) has no shopId; its id is sha1(sourcePath|page|box). POST /api/figures only checks that some FactorySetting has that sourcePath and figurePage. It then upserts: any role creates the first copy, and any non-TECH user of any company replaces the image bytes (`update: user.role === "TECH" ? {} : { width, height, data }`). On the hosted multi-shop app, one company can therefore swap the timing/adjustment diagrams every other company's techs look at. Three things make the damage stick. Once a figure is stored, the UI shows it through 'Show figure' and never redraws or re-uploads it (manual-figure.tsx:131 and 147-163). /api/figures/[id] is served with `Cache-Control: private, max-age=31536000, immutable`, so browsers keep a bad copy for a year. The upload is also pushed to the hub (shareFigure), where the first write wins. Other problems in the same handler: `box` is never matched against the setting's figureBox (any number of extra 1.5 MB rows can be stored per known page), the JPEG bytes are not checked, and a non-array box raises a 500.
failure_scenario: Shop A (a self-signed-up company on a hosted install, or any tenant) posts a wrong or offensive JPEG for sourcePath 'Sewing\Baby-Lock\...\BL-BL137A-ServiceManual.pdf', page 202, box [0,0.016,1,0.589]. Every other company's 'Show figure' for that hook-timing setting now displays shop A's image, and techs adjust machines from the wrong diagram.
suggested_fix: Accept only the exact figure a setting defines: look up the FactorySetting by sourcePath + figurePage and require figureId(sourcePath, page, setting.figureBox) === id. On an install with more than one company, allow replacing an existing figure only for isInstallAdmin/platform admin, or store figures per shop (add shopId and read own-then-shared). Check the JPEG magic bytes. Drop `immutable`, or version the URL, so a corrected figure reaches browsers.
evidence:
Scratch instance (:5140, own DB). figure-overwrite.js logs in as the owner of 'Hosting Co' and uploads LEGIT bytes, signs up a separate company 'Evil Two', uploads EVIL bytes for the same figure, then reads it back as Hosting Co:
```
victim upload 200 {"id":"aae4e923af070de1146f8be9"}
attacker (owner of another shop) upload 200 {"id":"aae4e923af070de1146f8be9"}
victim now sees: 200 EVIL-REPLACEMENT-FROM-OTHER-SHOP
```
route.ts:33-37: `await db.figureImage.upsert({ where: { id }, create: {...}, update: user.role === "TECH" ? {} : { width, height, data } });`
verifier_notes: confirmed: FigureImage has no shopId, and /api/figures/[id] serves the one install-wide row to every signed-in user of any company. POST /api/figures checks only that some FactorySetting has that sourcePath and figurePage. It then upserts with `update: user.role === "TECH" ? {} : {width,height,data}` (route.ts:33-37), so the owner or admin of any company can replace a figure every other company sees. The overwrite branch was introduced by round 1 (8b3e5f2 changed `update: {}` to the role-based update). That makes it a round-1 regression on multi-shop installs. Before round 1, any user could still plant the first copy. The stated purpose of the round-1 change (an owner or admin redrawing it from the manual replaces a wrong one) cannot be reached from the UI: manual-figure.tsx only calls saveOnline when `!stored`, so in practice only a crafted POST can replace a stored figure. model-info.ts computes figureStored from figureId(setting box), and the component renders /api/figures/<id>, so victims see the replaced image. It is served with `private, max-age=31536000, immutable`. Also confirmed: box is not tied to the setting's figureBox (arbitrary extra rows are stored), and a non-array box gives a 500. Medium, not high: the target is install-shared reference imagery, not another shop's business records.

security: src/app/api/figures/route.ts:28 POST /api/figures trusts the client's box, so any signed-in user can create unlimited 1.5 MB figure rows and push each one to the hub
code: src/app/api/figures/route.ts:36 FigureImage is one global table: any company's owner/admin can replace the manual figure every other company sees (and any tech can plant the first copy)
code: src/app/api/figures/route.ts:33 Shared manual figures can be planted or overwritten by any company's users (cross-tenant), and the round-1 'owner replaces a wrong figure' fix does not work

title: Local manuals folder: permission is requested after the click's user activation is consumed or expired, so Open and Save-scan fail after a browser restart
description: openLocal() calls `window.open("", "_blank")` first. In Chromium that consumes the click's transient activation. It then calls fileAt() -> ensurePermission() -> `h.requestPermission()`. When a restored directory handle's permission is back to 'prompt' (after a browser restart, unless 'Allow on every visit' was chosen), Chrome/Edge reject requestPermission without transient activation. The code comments themselves say 'Browsers may re-ask after a restart'. saveToLibrary() has the same problem: it asks for 'readwrite' only after the scanner has built the PDF, which takes several seconds for multi-page scans, so the activation has expired. ensurePermission() throws rather than returning false, so the download fallback (lines 247-253) is never reached. The only UI that requests 'readwrite' is connectFolder: Re-index requests just 'read'.
failure_scenario: On a hosted install (manuals come only from each PC's connected folder), a tech restarts Chrome and clicks Open on a machine's manual. The new tab closes and the toast says 'User activation is required to request permissions.' This repeats on every click until they happen to use Show figure or Re-index. Saving a multi-page scan fails the same way every time until they Forget and reconnect the folder.
suggested_fix: In the click handler, call queryPermission first and, if needed, requestPermission before window.open. If a prompt was shown, open the file in the same tab or ask for one more click. Request 'readwrite' at the very start of the scanner's Save click, before building the PDF. Make ensurePermission catch SecurityError and return false so saveToLibrary falls back to download.
evidence: Playwright/Chromium, measured in a click handler: {before: true, popup: true, after: false}, i.e. navigator.userActivation.isActive is false right after window.open('', '_blank'). Code: local-manuals.ts:206 `const w = window.open("", "_blank");` then 208 `await fileAt(path)` -> 192 `ensurePermission(root, "read")` -> 79 `await h.requestPermission({ mode })`. saveToLibrary line 230 `if (root && (await ensurePermission(root, "readwrite")))` runs after scanner.tsx builds the PDF. Not reproduced end to end: headless Playwright cannot return a directory handle from showDirectoryPicker.
verifier_notes: confirmed: openLocal (local-manuals.ts:206) calls window.open('', '_blank') before fileAt(), and fileAt() calls ensurePermission, which calls requestPermission. I measured in Chromium that window.open consumes the click's transient activation. FileSystemHandle.requestPermission requires transient activation when the state is 'prompt', and throws SecurityError without it. That is the state a stored directory handle returns to after a browser restart unless 'Allow on every visit' was chosen, and the code's own canReadWithoutPrompt comment says browsers re-ask after a restart. The failure path is concrete. ensurePermission throws rather than returning false, openLocal closes the tab and rethrows, and the caller shows a toast. The same applies to saveToLibrary. It asks for 'readwrite' only after scanner.tsx has built the PDF page by page, so for slow multi-page builds the 5 s activation window has passed. The throw then skips the download fallback at lines 247-253. rescan() asks only for 'read', so the only way back to readwrite is to reconnect the folder. This affects hosted or browser users who use a connected folder. The Windows program uses the server library path instead.
